speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I am Dr. Agent. I understand you are experiencing dizziness, nausea, and imbalance; to help me understand the nature of your symptoms, could you describe exactly how the dizziness feels, such as whether it is a spinning sensation or more like lightheadedness?

speaker: Patient
text: 27-year-old male. The patient reports a sustained sensation of the room spinning since this morning, which is low grade and constant. He occasionally feels nauseous and has taken diphenhydramine to help him sleep, which also alleviates his symptoms slightly. He mentions recent increased intake of garlic due to trying to recover from a cold a few days ago. Past medical history is unremarkable.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Vestibular Neuritis. The patient's description of a constant, spinning sensation (vertigo) that is relieved by antihistamines, combined with a lack of other focal neurological deficits mentioned in the history, strongly points to inflammation of the vestibular nerve rather than a central cause like a stroke or labyrinthitis (which would typically include hearing loss). The recent garlic intake is likely a red herring or mild irritant rather than the primary cause. Since I have determined the diagnosis, I will not ask further questions.
